# Employee Attrition and Income Analysis

This project explores relationships between employee characteristics, attrition and monthly income using the IBM HR Analytics dataset.

## 1. Data Import and Inspection

Load the dataset and inspect its dimensions and structure.

```{r data-import}
hrdata <- read.csv("HR-Employee-Attrition.csv")

dim(hrdata)
head(hrdata)
str(hrdata)
```

## 2. Correlation Analysis

Examine relationships between selected numerical variables. Education is stored as an ordinal numerical code, so correlations involving this variable should be interpreted cautiously.

```{r correlation}
# Create a list of numeric columns
num_cols <- c(
  "Age", "DailyRate", "DistanceFromHome",
  "Education", "HourlyRate", "MonthlyIncome",
  "MonthlyRate", "NumCompaniesWorked",
  "TotalWorkingYears", "TrainingTimesLastYear"
)

# Filter the data
hrdata_num <- hrdata[, num_cols]

# Calculate the correlation matrix
cor(hrdata_num)
```

## 3. Scatterplot Analysis

First, examine monthly income, age and education. Education is an ordinal variable, so its values appear in discrete bands.

```{r scatterplot-education}
pairs(
  ~ MonthlyIncome + Age + Education,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Income, Age and Education"
)
```

Next, replace education with total working years to compare three numerical variables.

```{r scatterplot-experience}
pairs(
  ~ MonthlyIncome + Age + TotalWorkingYears,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Income, Age and Working Experience"
)
```

## 4. Education-Level Analysis

Convert the education codes into labelled categories.

```{r education-categories}
hrdata$EducationLabel <- factor(
  hrdata$Education,
  levels = 1:5,
  labels = c(
    "Below College",
    "College",
    "Bachelor",
    "Master",
    "Doctor"
  ),
  ordered = TRUE
)

table(hrdata$EducationLabel, useNA = "ifany")
```

### Age by Education Level

```{r education-age}
boxplot(
  Age ~ EducationLabel,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Age by Education Level",
  xlab = "Education",
  ylab = "Age",
  outline = TRUE,
  pch = 1
)
```

### Working Experience by Education Level

```{r education-experience}
boxplot(
  TotalWorkingYears ~ EducationLabel,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Total Working Years by Education Level",
  xlab = "Education",
  ylab = "Total Working Years",
  outline = TRUE,
  pch = 1
)
```

### Monthly Income by Education Level

```{r education-income}
boxplot(
  MonthlyIncome ~ EducationLabel,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Monthly Income by Education Level",
  xlab = "Education",
  ylab = "Monthly Income",
  outline = TRUE,
  pch = 1
)
```

## 5. Employee Attrition and Age

Investigate whether employees who left the organisation differ in age from those who remained.

### Age Distribution by Attrition

```{r attrition-boxplot}
boxplot(
  Age ~ Attrition,
  data = hrdata,
  main = "Age Distribution by Attrition",
  xlab = "Attrition Status",
  ylab = "Age"
)
```

### Independent-Samples t-Test

Test whether the mean age differs between employees with and without attrition.

```{r attrition-ttest}
yes_age <- hrdata[
  hrdata$Attrition == "Yes", "Age"
]

no_age <- hrdata[
  hrdata$Attrition == "No", "Age"
]

t.test(yes_age, no_age)
```

The default Welch two-sample t-test evaluates whether the group means differ while allowing for unequal variances.

## 6. Simple Linear Regression

Examine the relationship between employee age and monthly income.

```{r simple-regression}
model1 <- lm(
  MonthlyIncome ~ Age,
  data = hrdata
)

summary(model1)
```

## 7. Multiple Linear Regression

Extend the model by including total working years alongside age.

This allows us to examine the association between age and monthly income while accounting for employees' accumulated working experience, and vice versa.

```{r multiple-regression}
model2 <- lm(
  MonthlyIncome ~ Age + TotalWorkingYears,
  data = hrdata
)

summary(model2)
```

## 8. Interpretation and Limitations

The statistical results above should be interpreted by examining group means, effect sizes, p-values, confidence intervals and regression coefficients.

The analysis is observational. Associations do not establish causality, and omitted variables may influence the observed relationships.

The next stage is to interpret the actual statistical outputs and summarise the findings.
